title: Process Injection: Proc Memory
summary: This sub-technique injects code by abusing the proc filesystem, the Linux interface that exposes kernel and process state as files. Each running process has a directory named after its numeric process identifier, and inside it the memory map file lists every mapped region with its start and end address and its permissions. An attacker reads that file to learn where the program's own code, its libraries and its stack live, which recovers the layout that address space layout randomisation was meant to hide, and then picks short instruction sequences already present in those mappings to build a return oriented programming chain, which is a payload assembled from fragments of the program itself rather than from new code. The write itself can be done with ordinary tools that write to a file offset, so no specialised injection library is needed and no unusual system call stands out. The aftermath is compression or overwriting of the target's stack or mappings, and the process may crash or behave erratically. Detection rests on file access auditing for the process memory and map files of other processes, on the fact that very few legitimate programs read another process's map file, and on memory evidence such as a stack that no longer matches a legitimate call chain.

beginner.definition: The proc filesystem is a folder called proc. It shows live information about a Linux system, including one folder per running process. This sub-technique is when an attacker reads those files to learn where a process keeps its code and data. They then write over part of that memory. It is part of the Process Injection parent technique. The difference is that the attacker uses simple file access instead of a special control call.
beginner.whyItMatters: Writing to a process through the filesystem looks like an ordinary file write, so unusual calls do not stand out. The technique also defeats one common protection by revealing the real memory addresses. Programs can crash afterwards, which may be mistaken for a software fault rather than an intrusion. Knowing that these files exist helps you audit who reads them.
howItWorks: The attacker finds the numeric identifier of the process they want to use.
They read the memory map file for that process, which lists each region, its address range and its permissions.
From those addresses they locate useful short instruction sequences inside existing code.
They assemble a payload from those fragments, so the new behaviour is built from the program's own instructions.
They write over part of the target's memory. They use a normal tool that writes to a chosen position in a file.
The target then runs the altered instructions, and often becomes unstable or crashes.
beginner.example: Think of a printed instruction booklet stapled together. Someone photographs the table of contents to learn which page holds which step. Then they tear out two pages and staple in different ones taken from elsewhere in the same book. The booklet still looks like the original and uses only its own paper. The reader follows the new order without noticing the swap. Only a careful page count shows that something was replaced.
takeaways: The proc filesystem reveals memory layout that is otherwise hidden.
A write through these files can look like an ordinary file operation.
Audit reads of another process's memory map to catch the preparation stage.

objectives: Explain what the proc filesystem exposes about a running process.
Describe how memory map information defeats address randomisation.
Explain what a return oriented payload is, in plain behavioural terms.
Identify the file access and memory telemetry that reveals this activity.
Explain why crash symptoms after this technique can be misread as a software fault.
